### 2.7

```{r}
# a.
retail_ts |> autoplot(sales)

# b.
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
    subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The NSA series displays a prominent, sharp spike every December due to holiday shopping, followed by a drop in January. The SA series removes this predictable annual spike, smoothing out the basic seasonal swings so that the underlying economic trend and recessionary drops are clearer.

## 3. Data Transformation

### 3.1

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |> 
  mutate(log_volume = log(Volume))

can_gas |> 
  autoplot(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Log of Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    x = NULL, y = "log(Volume)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |> 
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |> 
  mutate(log_sales = log(sales)) |> 
  autoplot(log_sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Log of U.S. Not Seasonally Adjusted Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "log(Sales)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 3.2

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |> 
  mutate(
    growth_direct  = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),
    growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume)
  )

can_gas |> 
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth Rate (Direct)",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas <- can_gas |> 
  mutate(growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_logdiff))

can_gas |> 
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(
    title = "Approximation Error: Direct vs Log-Difference Growth",
    x = NULL, y = "Absolute Difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The absolute difference plot shows that the log-difference approximation is extremely close to the exact percentage growth rate when monthly changes are small.

### 3.3

```{r}
retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The NSA growth rate series is significantly noisier than the SA series because it still contains monthly jumps that repeat each year and create massive spikes. The SA series filters those out, leaving a cleaner picture of monthly economic momentum.

## 4. Seeing, Decomposing, and Modeling Seasonality

### 4.1

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The SA plot is much flatter than the NSA plot, indicating that the seasonal adjustment process has successfully removed the predictable annual spikes and drops, leaving a more stable series.

```{r}
can_gas |> 
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Log of Canadian Natural Gas Production",
    y = "log(Volume)", x = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 4.2

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production",
    y = "log(Volume)"
  )
```

### 4.3

```{r}
# install.packages("seasonal")

retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()

retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()
```

The Month with the highest seasonal factor seems to be in the spring or summer, and the lowest around the winter. The trend component shows a small decrease in amplitude over time, especially after 2020.

```{r}
sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
    x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

When compared against the Census Bureau's official seasonally adjusted series, our custom X-13 adjustment matches extremely closely. Minor discrepancies only appear around specific holiday timing shifts or major economic turning points.

### 4.4

```{r}
can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))

report(can_gas_fit)

can_gas_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Estimated average monthly growth rate for Canadian gas production comes from the trend coefficient, approximately 0.4%. The biggest seasonal effect occurs in June, with the largest absolute value t-statistic, -4.777.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()

can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24) |>
  kable()
```

Based on the tibble output, the residuals do not look like white noise; there is a visible structure and autocorrelation left in them that could be modeled further. The Ljung–Box test yields a p-value of 0, leading us to strongly reject the null hypothesis of white noise at the 5% significance level and conclude that significant predictable patterns remain in the model.

### 5. A First Forecast Evaluation

## 5.1

```{r}
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  kable()
```

The Seasonal Naive model forecasts significantly more accurately than the TSLM model, yielding much lower error values. Both the MAE and RMSE metrics support this conclusion.

### 5.2

```{r}
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()

forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)
```

The Diebold-Mariano test shows a highly significant difference in forecast accuracy between the two models, with the negative DM statistic confirming that the seasonal naive model yields significantly smaller forecast errors than the tslm model.

### 5.3

```{r}
gas_rolling_fc <- can_gas |> 
  select(Month, Volume) |> 
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |> 
  model(
    snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
    tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())
  ) |> 
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_rolling_fc |> 
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE)) |>
  kable()
```
